clue.text: Outlaw who was just, still, in trouble, and always eleven

definitions.meaning: leader of the gang of boys calling themselves the Outlaws in Richmal Crompton's stories

definitions.text: who was just, still, in trouble, and always eleven
definitions.meaning: echoes the book titles Just William, Still William and William in Trouble, whose hero never ages past eleven

explanation.surface: A description of some reformed bandit who never grew up and kept landing in scrapes.
explanation.walkthrough: Richmal Crompton's children's books, popular in Britain since the 1920s, have titles like Just William, Still William and William in Trouble; their schoolboy hero stays eleven throughout.
explanation.definitionFit: Both halves describe Crompton's schoolboy hero: gang leader of the Outlaws and title figure of the Just, Still and In Trouble books.

clue.text: Greyfriars Harry

parts.note: Greyfriars is the boarding school in Frank Richards's schoolboy stories, and Harry is the captain of the Remove there

explanation.definitionFit: Frank Richards named the head boy of Greyfriars's Famous Five Harry, giving him this surname in the Magnet stories.

clue.text: Put up a poet

Thomas ... was an Elizabethan poet and dramatist, author of Rosalynde

explanation.definitionFit: To house a guest is to put them up; Thomas Lodge was an Elizabethan writer of verse and romances.

clue.text: Monies due in new production for Mozart hero

indicators.note: a new production stages the same material afresh, so these letters are rearranged into a fresh order

explanation.surface: Money owed on a fresh staging of a Mozart opera about its title hero.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in new production' signals the anagram of MONIES DUE; the theatrical phrase fits the opera surface neatly.
explanation.definitionFit: Mozart's opera seria Idomeneo has the King of Crete as its title figure, in Greek form spelled with this ending.

clue.text: Space traveller's self-identification is pidgin, but suitable

explanation.walkthrough: The alien introduces himself Tarzan-style, so the pidgin self-introduction comes first; 'but' is a link to the old sense of the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Meet is an old word for fitting or proper, as in 'it is meet and right'.

clue.text: Sweet religion makes / A of words " (Hamlet)

definitions.text: Sweet religion makes / A of words " (Hamlet)

parts.words: Sweet religion makes / A of words " (Hamlet)
parts.note: a quotation from Hamlet's rebuke of Gertrude with its key noun left out for the solver to supply

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet tells his mother that her broken vows make sweet religion a mere string of empty words; the missing word is a musical or literary term for effusive outpouring.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's line uses the word for an ecstatic, rambling outpouring, here meaning a meaningless jumble of fine-sounding speech.

clue.text: Foot is part of anchor, I am bound to say

indicators.note: the letters wanted are only a portion of the words that follow, running across them

explanation.surface: Someone confessing that a foot really is part of an anchor.

explanation.definitionFit: In prosody a foot is a metrical unit, and this one is a trochee joined to an iamb.
